title: Pretexting: when the story is the attack
body_md:
## When the story is the tool

A pretext is a made-up role and situation that makes a request seem like the next routine step. It may borrow a real organization, a real event or details about you. The caller’s knowledge of an address or the last digits of an account is not proof of identity: such details may be public, stolen or guessed. Caller ID can also be altered. What matters is the requested action and whether you can confirm it outside the conversation.

A convincing story fits a routine: a delivery needs an address, payroll needs a form, IT needs an update, a bank needs to handle a disputed transaction. The attacker asks for a seemingly small step, then uses your cooperation to justify the next. A “fraud officer” might first ask whether a charge is yours, then insist that you move money to a “safe” account. Answering an initial question is not a commitment to follow the rest of the script.

A pretext may also explain away the very safeguard you would normally use: “the app is down,” “we cannot put this in writing,” or “don’t call the main desk because this case is confidential.” These explanations are claims, not proof. Real exceptions can happen; verify through the institution’s established app, the number on a card or statement, or a known internal directory. Tell that independent contact the exact claim and ask whether an action is required. Do not use callback details supplied by the person whose identity you are checking.

**Break contact without diagnosing the caller.** You do not need to prove a lie while on the line. Record only non-sensitive basics such as the claimed organization and issue, end the interaction, and independently check. If the matter is real, the organization can explain the next steps through its normal channel. If you already sent information or money, contact the relevant provider promptly using a trusted channel; options vary by country and payment method.

The examples show why a realistic administrative story still requires a clean verification path. The practice rehearses that path through a fictional benefits-office call.

widget_config.goal: Extract the request from a plausible cover story and confirm it through an independently chosen channel.
widget_config.today_action: Save one trusted contact route for a bank or workplace service before you need it; use an existing card, app or directory.
widget_config.scope: General technique; FTC callback advice is US consumer guidance and NCSC advice is UK guidance. Use your own institution’s real process and local response channels.

blocks.title: Synthetic: “card safety desk”
blocks.situation: An inbound caller displays the bank’s name, knows your street, and describes an unfamiliar hotel charge. After you say it was not yours, the caller asks you to transfer your balance into a temporary protected account.
blocks.analysis: The first question resembles a legitimate fraud check; the transfer is the consequential step. Neither displayed name nor personal detail authenticates the caller. End the call and check the charge in your own banking app or call the number on your card. Never treat a caller-directed transfer as account protection.

blocks.title: Synthetic: real payroll form
blocks.situation: A known HR colleague mentions that employees must update tax details after a company merger. The same notice appears in the authenticated staff portal, and your manager confirms the deadline through a contact you already use.
blocks.analysis: An administrative request and a deadline can be real. The established portal and independent confirmation support the story. Enter details only through the verified workplace process; do not email documents in reply to an unexpected message.

blocks.title: The benefits-office story
blocks.setup: A fictional caller says a routine benefits record failed to import. The exercise contains no real identity details.

steps.prompt: The caller knows your department and asks you to “confirm” a personal identifier. What do you do?

choices.text: Provide it; knowing the department proves the caller belongs there.
choices.consequence: You expose information without authenticating the caller.
choices.explanation: Workplace details may be available from public profiles or a compromised directory.

choices.text: Ask for the claimed office and issue, then end the call without giving the identifier.
choices.consequence: You preserve enough context to check independently.
choices.explanation: You can verify a claim without continuing the caller’s workflow.

steps.prompt: After you disclose the identifier, the caller says the normal portal is down and dictates an alternate upload link. What now?

choices.text: Stop, end the call, and call the real benefits desk using the existing staff directory.
choices.consequence: You can still interrupt the script and reach a real service.
choices.explanation: Even after one disclosure, do not compound it; tell verified staff what happened.

choices.text: Use the dictated link to finish quickly.
choices.consequence: You expose more details through an unverified page.
choices.explanation: The asserted outage and link both come from the same unverified caller.

steps.prompt: After you end the call, a text claims the staff portal is down and offers an alternate upload link. What now?

choices.text: Open the new link; it arrived by a different channel.
choices.consequence: The second message may be part of the same operation.
choices.explanation: A second inbound channel is not independent verification.

choices.text: Call the real benefits desk using the number already in your staff directory.
choices.consequence: The claimed outage is checked outside both inbound contacts.
choices.explanation: Ask the real service whether the request exists before submitting anything.

steps.prompt: The real benefits desk says no update is due. What next?

choices.text: Do not submit; report the contact and any information already shared through your workplace’s verified response route.
choices.consequence: The request stops, and verified staff can advise on any exposed information.
choices.explanation: Use the established confidential process to describe what was shared; avoid posting identifiers or the unverified link in a public channel.

choices.text: Ignore the desk because the caller sounded more confident.
choices.consequence: You privilege tone over an independent record.
choices.explanation: Confidence and detailed scripts do not outrank the actual account or service owner.

steps.prompt: The unverified upload page asks for more personal documents. You may also have disclosed an identifier by phone. What now?

choices.text: Upload the documents to complete the caller’s request.
choices.consequence: More sensitive information may reach the same unverified party.
choices.explanation: Opening a page or sharing one identifier does not establish that the request is legitimate.

choices.text: Stop using the page; contact the real benefits desk through the existing directory and explain any information already shared.
choices.consequence: You interrupt further disclosure and can ask the real service about protective steps.
choices.explanation: The independent desk can check whether an update exists and advise on an exposed identifier; avoid the caller’s link and number.

blocks.debrief: Debrief: disclosing the identifier changes what you may need to report. Opening an unverified page never yields the real desk’s answer; only using the established route does. Replay to practise stopping after any exposure and telling verified staff what happened.

questions.prompt: A caller knows the last four digits of your card. Does that prove the caller is the bank?

choices.text: Yes; only the bank could know them.
choices.explanation: Partial account details can leak or be obtained elsewhere.

choices.text: No; independently reach the bank before acting.
choices.explanation: Correct: identity comes from a trusted contact path, not a fact recited by the inbound caller.

questions.prompt: A delivery company’s real app shows a parcel awaiting address correction. What is a reasonable next step?

choices.text: Use the app’s own help flow, after opening it yourself.
choices.explanation: Correct: a legitimate issue can be handled without the text’s link.

choices.text: Send the address and card details to the caller so they can fix it.
choices.explanation: That leaves the verified channel and exposes data unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: The caller says the usual verification process is unavailable. Best interpretation?

choices.explanation: Outages can be real; the claim still needs checking.

choices.text: Treat it as an unverified claim and ask the established service channel.
choices.explanation: Correct: neither automatically accept nor dismiss the entire issue.
